arXiv:1705.06908v1 [cs.LG] 19 May 2017

Unbiased estimates for linear regression
via volume sampling

Michał Dereziński Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: University of California Santa Cruz Email: mderezin@ucsc.edu    Manfred K. Warmuth Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: University of California Santa Cruz Email: manfred@ucsc.edu
Abstract

Given a full rank matrix 𝐗\mathbf{X} with more columns than rows consider the task of estimating the pseudo inverse 𝐗+\mathbf{X}^{+} based on the pseudo inverse of a sampled subset of columns (of size at least the number of rows). We show that this is possible if the subset of columns is chosen proportional to the squared volume spanned by the rows of the chosen submatrix (ie, volume sampling). The resulting estimator is unbiased and surprisingly the covariance of the estimator also has a closed form: It equals a specific factor times 𝐗+​𝐗+⁣⊤\mathbf{X}^{+}\mathbf{X}^{+\top}.

Pseudo inverse plays an important part in solving the linear least squares problem, where we try to predict a label for each column of 𝐗\mathbf{X}. We assume labels are expensive and we are only given the labels for the small subset of columns we sample from 𝐗\mathbf{X}. Using our methods we show that the weight vector of the solution for the sub problem is an unbiased estimator of the optimal solution for the whole problem based on all column labels.

We believe that these new formulas establish a fundamental connection between linear least squares and volume sampling. We use our methods to obtain an algorithm for volume sampling that is faster than state-of-the-art and for obtaining bounds for the total loss of the estimated least-squares solution on all labeled columns.

   

1 Introduction

Let 𝐗\mathbf{X} be a wide full rank matrix with dd rows and nn columns where n≥dn\geq d. Our goal is to estimate the pseudo inverse 𝐗+\mathbf{X}^{+} of 𝐗\mathbf{X} based on the pseudo inverse of a subset of columns. More precisely, we sample a subset S⊆{1..n}S\subseteq\{1..n\} of ss column indices (where s≥ds\geq d). We let 𝐗S\mathbf{X}_{S} be the sub-matrix of the ss columns indexed by SS (See Figure 1). Consider a version of 𝐗\mathbf{X} in which all but the columns of SS are zero. This matrix equals 𝐗𝐈S\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S} where 𝐈S\mathbf{I}_{S} is an nn-dimensional diagonal matrix with (𝐈S)i​i=1(\mathbf{I}_{S})_{ii}=1 if i∈Si\in S and 0 otherwise.

We assume that the set of ss column indices of 𝐗\mathbf{X} is selected proportional to the squared volume spanned by the rows of submatrix 𝐗S\mathbf{X}_{S}, i.e. proportional to det(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)\det(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top}) and prove a number of new surprising expectation formulas for this type of volume sampling, such as

𝔼⁡[(𝐗𝐈S)+]=𝐗+and𝔼⁡[(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)−1⏟(𝐗𝐈S)+⁣⊤​(𝐗𝐈S)+]=n−d+1s−d+1​𝐗+⁣⊤​𝐗+.\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+}]=\mathbf{X}^{+}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathbb{E}[\underbrace{(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})^{-1}}_{(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+\top}(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+}}]=\frac{n-d+1}{s-d+1}\,\mathbf{X}^{+\top}\mathbf{X}^{+}.

Note that (𝐗𝐈S)+(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+} has the n×dn\times d shape of 𝐗+\mathbf{X}^{+} where the ss rows indexed by SS contain (𝐗S)+(\mathbf{X}_{S})^{+} and the remaining n−sn-s rows are zero. The expectation of this matrix is 𝐗+\mathbf{X}^{+} even though (𝐗S)+(\mathbf{X}_{S})^{+} is clearly not a sub-matrix of 𝐗+\mathbf{X}^{+}. In addition to the expectation formulas, our new techniques lead to an efficient volume sampling procedure which beats the state-of-the-art by a factor of n2n^{2} in time complexity.

Volume sampling is useful in numerous applications, from clustering to matrix approximation, but we focus on the task of solving linear least squares problems: For an n−n-dimensional label vector 𝐲\mathbf{y}, let 𝐰∗=argmin𝐰‖𝐗⊤​𝐰−𝐲‖2=𝐗+​𝐲\mathbf{w}^{*}=\argmin_{\mathbf{w}}||\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{y}||^{2}=\mathbf{X}^{+}\mathbf{y}. Assume the entire design matrix 𝐗\mathbf{X} is known to the learner but labels are expensive and you want to observe as few of them as possible. Let 𝐰S∗=𝐗S+​𝐲S\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*}=\mathbf{X}_{S}^{+}\mathbf{y}_{S} be the solution to the sub-problem based on labels 𝐲S\mathbf{y}_{S}. What is the smallest number of labels ss necessary, for which there is a sampling procedure on sets SS of size ss st the expected loss of 𝐰S∗\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*} is at most a constant factor larger than the loss of 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*} that uses all nn labels (where the constant is independent of nn)? More precisely, using the short hand L⁡(𝐰)=‖𝐗⊤​𝐰−𝐲‖2L(\mathbf{w})=||\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{y}||^{2} for the loss on all nn labels, what is the smallest size ss such that 𝔼⁡[L⁡(𝐰S∗)]≤const​L​(𝐰∗)\mathbb{E}[L(\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*})]\leq\text{const}\,L(\mathbf{w}^{*}). This question is a version of the “minimal coresets” open problem posed in [2].

The size has to be at least dd and one can show that randomization is necessary in that any deterministic algorithm for choosing a set of dd columns can suffer loss larger by a factor of nn. Also any iid sampling of SS (such as the commonly used leverage scores [7]) requires at least Ω⁡(d​log⁡d)\Omega(d\log d) examples to achieve a finite factor. In this paper however we show that with a size dd volume sample, 𝔼⁡[L⁡(𝐰S∗)]=(d+1)​L​(𝐰∗)\mathbb{E}[L(\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*})]=(d+1)L(\mathbf{w}^{*}) if 𝐗\mathbf{X} is in general position. Note again that we have an equality and not just an upper bound. Also we can show that the mulitplicative factor d+1d+1 is optimal. We further improve this factor to 1+ϵ1+\epsilon through repeated volume sampling. Moreover, our expectation formulas imply that when SS is a volume sampled set of size s≥ds\geq d, then 𝐰S∗\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*} is an unbiased estimator for 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*}, ie 𝔼⁡[𝐰S∗]=𝐰∗\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*}]=\mathbf{w}^{*}.

2 Related Work

Volume sampling is an extension of a determinantal point process [13], which has been given a lot of attention in the literature with many applications to machine learning, including recommendation systems [9] and clustering [11]. Many exact and approximate methods for efficiently generating samples from this distribution have been proposed [5, 12], making it a useful tool in the design of randomized algorithms. Most of those methods focus on sampling s≤ds\leq d elements. In this paper, we study volume sampling sets of size s≥ds\geq d, which has been proposed in [1] and motivated with applications in graph theory, linear regression, matrix approximation and more. The only known polynomial time algorithm for size s>ds>d volume sampling was recently proposed in [14] with time complexity O⁡(n4​s)O(n^{4}s). We offer a new algorithm with runtime O⁡((n−s+d)​n​d)O((n-s+d)nd), which is faster by a factor of at least n2n^{2}.

The problem of selecting a subset of input vectors for solving a linear regression task has been extensively studied in statistics literature under the terms optimal design [8] and pool-based active learning [16]. Various criteria for subset selection have been proposed, like A-optimality and D-optimality. For example, A-optimality seeks to minimize tr⁡((𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)−1)\mathrm{tr}((\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})^{-1}), which is combinatorially hard to optimize exactly. We show that for size ss volume sampling (for s≥ds\geq d), 𝔼⁡[(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)−1]=n−d+1s−d+1​𝐗+⁣⊤​𝐗+\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})^{-1}]=\frac{n-d+1}{s-d+1}\,\mathbf{X}^{+\top}\mathbf{X}^{+} which provides an approximate randomized solution for this task.

A related task has been explored in the field of computational geometry, where efficient algorithms are sought for approximately solving linear regression and matrix approximation [15, 4, 2]. Here, subsampling appears as one of the key techniques for obtaining multiplicative bounds on the loss of the approximate solution. In this line of work, volume sampling size s≤ds\leq d has been used by [6, 10] for matrix approximation. Another common sampling technique is based on statistical leverage scores [7], which have been effectively used for the task of linear regression. However, this approach is based on iid sampling, and requires sampling at least Ω⁡(d​log⁡d)\Omega(d\log d) elements to achieve multiplicative loss bounds. On the other hand, the input vectors obtained from volume sampling are selected jointly, which makes the chosen subset more informative, and we show that just dd volume sampled elements are sufficient to achieve a multiplicative bound.

3 Unbiased estimators

Let nn be an integer dimension. For each subset S⊆{1..n}S\subseteq\{1..n\} of size ss we are given a matrix formula 𝐅S\mathbf{F}_{S}. Our goal is to sample set SS of size ss using some sampling process and then develop concise expressions for 𝔼S:|S|=s[𝐅S]\mathbb{E}_{S:|S|=s}[\mathbf{F}_{S}]. Examples of formula classes 𝐅S\mathbf{F}_{S} will be given below.

We represent the sampling by a directed acyclic graph (dag), with a single root node corresponding to the full set {1..n}\{1..n\}, Starting from the root, we proceed along the edges of the graph, iteratively removing elements from the set SS. Concretely, consider a dag with levels s=n,n−1,…,ds=n,n-1,...,d. Level ss contains (ns)n\choose s nodes for sets S⊆{1..n}S\subseteq\{1..n\} of size ss. Every node SS at level s>ds>d has ss directed edges to the nodes S−{i}S-\{i\} at the next lower level. These edges are labeled with a conditional probability vector P⁡(i|S)P(i|S). The probability of a (directed) path is the product of the probabilities along its edges. The outflow of probability from each node on all but the bottom level is 1. We let the probability P⁡(S)P(S) of node SS be the probability of all paths from the top node {1..n}\{1..n\} to SS and set the probability P({1..n})P(\{1..n\}) of the top node to 1. We associate a formula 𝐅S\mathbf{F}_{S} with each set node SS in the dag. The following key equality lets us compute expectations, where we use S±iS_{\pm i} as SS with element ii added/subtracted.

Lemma 1

If for all S⊆{1..n}S\subseteq\{1..n\} of size greater than dd we have

𝐅S=∑i∈SP⁡(i|S)​𝐅S−i,\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\mathbf{F}_{S}=\sum_{i\in S}P(i|S)\mathbf{F}_{S_{-i}}}\color[rgb]{0,0,0},

then for any s∈{d..n}s\in\{d..n\}: 𝔼S:|S|=s[𝐅S]=∑S:|S|=sP(S)𝐅S=𝐅{1..n}.\;\;\mathbb{E}_{S:|S|=s}[\mathbf{F}_{S}]=\sum_{S:|S|=s}P(S)\mathbf{F}_{S}=\mathbf{F}_{\{1..n\}}.

Proof  Suffices to show that expectations at successive layers are equal:

∑S:|S|=sP(S)𝐅S=∑S:|S|=s∑i∈SP(i|S)𝐅S−i=∑T:|T|=s−1∑j∉TP⁡(T+j)​P​(j|T+j)⏟P⁡(T)𝐅T. \sum_{S:|S|=s}P(S)\,\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\mathbf{F}_{S}}\color[rgb]{0,0,0}=\sum_{S:|S|=s}\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\sum_{i\in S}P(i|S)\,\mathbf{F}_{S_{-i}}}\color[rgb]{0,0,0}=\sum_{T:|T|=s-1}\underbrace{\sum_{j\notin T}P(T_{+j})P(j|T_{+j})}_{P(T)}\mathbf{F}_{T}.\qquad\rule{6.45831pt}{6.45831pt}

3.1 Volume sampling

Given a wide full-rank matrix 𝐗∈ℝd×n\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n} and a sample size s∈{d..n}s\in\{d..n\}, volume sampling chooses subset S⊆{1..n}S\subseteq\{1..n\} of size ss with probability proportional to volume spanned by the rows of submatrix 𝐗S\mathbf{X}_{S}, ie proportional to det(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)\det(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top}). The following corollary uses the above dag setup to compute the normalization constant for this distribution. When s=ds=d, the corollary provides a novel minimalist proof for the Cauchy-Binet formula: ∑S:|S|=sdet(𝐗S𝐗S⊤)=det(𝐗𝐗⊤)\sum_{S:|S|=s}\det(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})=\det(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^{\top}).

Corollary 2

Let 𝐗∈ℝd×n\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n} and S∈{1..n}S\in\{1..n\} of size n≥s≥dn\geq s\geq d st det(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)>0\det(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})>0. Then for any i∈Si\in S, define

P⁡(i|S):=det(𝐗S−i​𝐗S−i⊤)(s−d)​det(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)=1−𝐱i⊤​(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)−1​𝐱is−d,\displaystyle\hskip-5.69046ptP(i|S):=\frac{\det(\mathbf{X}_{S_{-i}}\mathbf{X}_{S_{-i}}^{\top})}{(s-d)\det(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})}=\frac{1-\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\top}(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{x}_{i}}{s-d}, (reverse iterative volume sampling)

where 𝐱i\mathbf{x}_{i} is the iith column of 𝐗\mathbf{X} and 𝐗S\mathbf{X}_{S} is the sub matrix of columns indexed by SS. Then P⁡(i|S)P(i|S) is a proper probability distribution and thus ∑S:|S|=sP(S)=1\sum_{S:|S|=s}P(S)=1 for all s∈{d..n}s\in\{d..n\}. Furthermore

P⁡(S)=det(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)(n−ds−d)​det(𝐗𝐗⊤).\displaystyle P(S)=\frac{\det(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})}{{n-d\choose s-d}\det(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^{\top})}. (volume sampling)

Proof  For any SS, st det(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)>0\det(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})>0, it is easy to see that P⁡(i|S)P(i|S) forms a probability vector:

∑i∈SP⁡(i|S)=∑i∈S1−tr⁡((𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)−1​𝐱i​𝐱i⊤)s−d=s−tr⁡((𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)−1​𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)s−d=s−ds−d=1.\sum_{i\in S}P(i|S)=\sum_{i\in S}\frac{1-\mathrm{tr}((\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{x}_{i}\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\top})}{s-d}=\frac{s-\mathrm{tr}((\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})}{s-d}=\frac{s-d}{s-d}=1.

It remains to show the formula for the probability P⁡(S)P(S) of all paths ending at 𝐅S\mathbf{F}_{S}. We first consider the top node, ie {1..n}\{1..n\}. In this case both the path definition and the formula are 1. For all but the top node, the probability P⁡(S)P(S) equals the total inflow of probability into that node from the previous level, ie

P⁡(S)=∑i∉SP⁡(i|S+i)​P​(S+i)\displaystyle P(S)=\sum_{i\notin S}P(i|{S_{+i}})\;P({S_{+i}}) =∑i∉Sdet(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)(s+1−d)​det(𝐗S+i​𝐗S+i⊤)​det(𝐗S+i​𝐗S+i⊤)(n−ds+1−d)​det(𝐗𝐗⊤)\displaystyle=\sum_{i\notin S}\frac{\det(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})}{(s+1-d)\cancel{\det(\mathbf{X}_{S_{+i}}\mathbf{X}_{S_{+i}}^{\top})}}\frac{\cancel{\det(\mathbf{X}_{S_{+i}}\mathbf{X}_{S_{+i}}^{\top})}}{{n-d\choose s+1-d}\det(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^{\top})}
=(n−s)​det(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)(s+1−d)​(n−ds+1−d)​det(𝐗𝐗⊤)=det(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)(n−ds−d)​det(𝐗𝐗⊤). \displaystyle=\frac{(n-s)\det(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})}{(s+1-d){n-d\choose s+1-d}\det(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^{\top})}=\frac{\det(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})}{{n-d\choose s-d}\det(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^{\top})}.\quad\quad\rule{6.45831pt}{6.45831pt}

Note that all paths from SS to a subset TT (of size ≥d\geq d) have the same probability because the ratios of determinants cancel along paths. Note that 00\frac{0}{0} ratios are avoided because paths with such ratios always lead to sets of probability 0.

3.2 Expectation formulas for volume sampling

All expectations in the remainder of the paper are wrt volume sampling. We use the short hand 𝔼⁡[𝐅S]\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{F}_{S}] for expectation with volume sampling where the size of the sampled set is fixed to ss. The expectation formulas for two choices of 𝐅S\mathbf{F}_{S} are proven in the next two theorems. By Lemma 1 it suffices to show 𝐅S=∑i∈SP⁡(i|S)​𝐅S−i\mathbf{F}_{S}=\sum_{i\in S}P(i|S)\mathbf{F}_{S_{-i}} for volume sampling.

We introduce a bit more notation first. Recall that 𝐗S\mathbf{X}_{S} is the sub matrix of columns indexed by S⊆{1..n}S\subseteq\{1..n\} (See Figure 1). Consider a version of 𝐗\mathbf{X} in which all but the columns of SS are zero. This matrix equals 𝐗𝐈S\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S} where 𝐈S\mathbf{I}_{S} is an nn-dimensional diagonal matrix with (𝐈S)i​i=1(\mathbf{I}_{S})_{ii}=1 if i∈Si\in S and 0 otherwise.

Theorem 3

Let 𝐗∈ℝd×n\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n} be a wide full rank matrix (ie n≥dn\geq d). For s∈{d..n}s\in\{d..n\}, let S⊆1..nS\subseteq 1..n be a size ss volume sampled set over 𝐗\mathbf{X}. Then

𝔼⁡[(𝐗𝐈S)+]=𝐗+.\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+}]=\mathbf{X}^{+}.

We believe that this fundamental formula lies at the core of why volume sampling is important in many applications. In this work, we focus on its application to linear regression. However, [1] discuss many problems where controlling the pseudo-inverse of a submatrix is essential. For those applications, it is important to establish variance bounds for the estimator offered by Theorem 3. In this case, volume sampling once again offers very concrete guarantees. We obtain them by showing the following formula, which can be viewed as a second moment for this estimator.

Theorem 4

Let 𝐗∈ℝd×n\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n} be a full-rank matrix and s∈{d..n}s\in\{d..n\}. If size ss volume sampling over 𝐗\mathbf{X} has full support, then

𝔼⁡[(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)−1⏟(𝐗𝐈S)+⁣⊤​(𝐗𝐈S)+]=n−d+1s−d+1​(𝐗𝐗⊤)−1⏟𝐗+⁣⊤​𝐗+.\mathbb{E}[\underbrace{(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})^{-1}}_{(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+\top}(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+}}]=\frac{n-d+1}{s-d+1}\,\underbrace{(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^{\top})^{-1}}_{\mathbf{X}^{+\top}\mathbf{X}^{+}}.

If volume sampling does not have full support then the matrix equality “==” is replaced by the positive-definite inequality “⪯\preceq”.

The condition that size ss volume sampling over 𝐗\mathbf{X} has full support is equivalent to det(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)>0\det(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})>0 for all S⊆1..nS\subseteq 1..n of size ss. Note that if size ss volume sampling has full support, then size t>st>s also has full support. So full support for the smallest size dd (often phrased as 𝐗\mathbf{X} being in general position) implies that volume sampling wrt any size s≥ds\geq d has full support.

Surprisingly by combining theorems 3 and 4, we can obtain a “covariance type formula” for the pseudo-inverse matrix estimator:

𝔼⁡[((𝐗𝐈S)+−𝔼⁡[(𝐗𝐈S)+])⊤​((𝐗𝐈S)+−𝔼⁡[(𝐗𝐈S)+])]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[((\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+}-\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+}])^{\top}\;((\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+}-\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+}])]
=𝔼⁡[(𝐗𝐈S)+⁣⊤​(𝐗𝐈S)+]−𝔼​[(𝐗𝐈S)+]⊤​𝔼​[(𝐗𝐈S)+]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+\top}(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+}]-\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+}]^{\top}\;\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+}]
=n−d+1s−d+1​𝐗+⁣⊤​𝐗+−𝐗+⁣⊤​𝐗+=n−ss−d+1​𝐗+⁣⊤​𝐗+.\displaystyle=\frac{n-d+1}{s-d+1}\;\mathbf{X}^{+\top}\mathbf{X}^{+}-\mathbf{X}^{+\top}\mathbf{X}^{+}=\frac{n-s}{s-d+1}\;\mathbf{X}^{+\top}\mathbf{X}^{+}. (1)

Theorem 4 can also be used to obtain an expectation formula for the Frobenius norm ‖(𝐗𝐈S)+‖F\|(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+}\|_{F} of the estimator:

𝔼​‖(𝐗𝐈S)+‖F2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+}\|_{F}^{2} =𝔼⁡[tr⁡((𝐗𝐈S)+⁣⊤​(𝐗𝐈S)+)]=n−d+1s−d+1​‖𝐗+‖F2.\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{tr}((\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+\top}(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+})]=\frac{n-d+1}{s-d+1}\|\mathbf{X}^{+}\|_{F}^{2}. (2)

This norm formula has been shown in [1], with numerous applications. Theorem 4 can be viewed as a much stronger pre trace version of the norm formula. Also our proof techniques are quite different and much simpler. Note that if size ss volume sampling for 𝐗\mathbf{X} does not have full support then (1) becomes a semi-definite inequality ⪯\preceq between matrices and (2) an inequality between numbers.

Proof of Theorem 3  We apply Lemma 1 with 𝐅S=(𝐗𝐈S)+\mathbf{F}_{S}=(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+}. It suffices to show 𝐅S=∑i∈SP⁡(i|S)​𝐅S−i\mathbf{F}_{S}=\sum_{i\in S}P(i|S)\mathbf{F}_{S_{-i}} for P⁡(i|S):=1−𝐱i⊤​(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)−1​𝐱is−dP(i|S):=\frac{1-\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\top}(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{x}_{i}}{s-d}, ie:

4 Linear regression with few labels

Our main motivation for studying volume sampling came from asking the following simple question. Suppose we want to solve a dd-dimensional linear regression problem with a matrix 𝐗∈ℝd×n\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n} of input column vectors and a label vector 𝐲∈ℝn\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, ie find 𝐰∈ℝd\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} that minimizes the least squares loss L⁡(𝐰)=‖𝐗⊤​𝐰−𝐲‖2L(\mathbf{w})=\|\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{y}\|^{2}:

𝐰∗=defargmin𝐰∈ℝdL​(𝐰)=𝐗+⁣⊤​𝐲,\mathbf{w}^{*}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{{def}}}}{{=}}\argmin_{\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}L(\mathbf{w})=\mathbf{X}^{+\top}\mathbf{y},

but the access to label vector 𝐲\mathbf{y} is restricted. We are allowed to pick a subset S⊆{1..n}S\subseteq\{1..n\} for which the labels yiy_{i} (where i∈Si\in S) are revealed to us, and then solve the subproblem (𝐗S,𝐲S)(\mathbf{X}_{S},\mathbf{y}_{S}), obtaining 𝐰S∗\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*}. What is the smallest number of labels such that for any 𝐗\mathbf{X}, we can find 𝐰S∗\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*} for which L⁡(𝐰S∗)L(\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*}) is only a multiplicative factor away from L⁡(𝐰∗)L(\mathbf{w}^{*}) (independent of the number of input vectors nn)? This question was posed as an open problem by [2]. It is easy to show that we need at least dd labels (when 𝐗\mathbf{X} is full-rank), so as to guarantee the uniqueness of solution 𝐰S∗\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*}. We show that dd labels are in fact sufficient, by using volume sampling to select the desired subset SS (proof in Section 4.1).

Theorem 5

If the input matrix 𝐗∈ℝd×n\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n} is in general position, then for any label vector 𝐲∈ℝn\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, the expected square loss (on all nn labeled vectors) of the optimal solution 𝐰S∗\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*} for the subproblem (𝐗S,𝐲S)(\mathbf{X}_{S},\mathbf{y}_{S}), with the dd-element set SS obtained from volume sampling, is given by

𝔼⁡[L⁡(𝐰S∗)]=(d+1)​L​(𝐰∗).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[L(\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*})]=(d+1)\;L(\mathbf{w}^{*}).

If 𝐗\mathbf{X} is not in general position, then the expected loss is upper-bounded by (d+1)​L​(𝐰∗)(d+1)\;L(\mathbf{w}^{*}).

The factor d+1d+1 cannot be improved when selecting only dd labels (we omit the proof):

Proposition 6

For any dd, there exists a least squares problem (𝐗,𝐲)(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y}) with d+1d+1 vectors in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} such that for every dd-element index set S⊆{1,…,d+1}S\subseteq\{1,...,d+1\}, we have

L⁡(𝐰S∗)=(d+1)​L​(𝐰∗).L(\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*})=(d+1)\;L(\mathbf{w}^{*}).

The multiplicative factor in Theorem 5 does not depend on nn. It is easy to see that this cannot be achieved by any deterministic algorithm (without the access to labels). Namely, suppose that d=1d=1 and 𝐗\mathbf{X} is a vector of all ones, whereas the label vector 𝐲\mathbf{y} is a vector of all ones except for a single zero. No matter which column index we choose deterministically, if that index corresponds to the label 00, the solution to the subproblem will incur loss L⁡(𝐰S∗)=n​L​(𝐰∗)L(\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*})=n\,L(\mathbf{w}^{*}). The fact that volume sampling is a joint distribution also plays an essential role in proving Theorem 5. Consider a matrix 𝐗\mathbf{X} with exactly dd unique linearly independent columns (and an arbitrary number of duplicates). Any iid column sampling distribution (like for example leverage score sampling) will require Ω⁡(d​log⁡d)\Omega(d\log d) samples to retrieve all dd unique columns (ie coupon collector problem), which is necessary to get any multiplicative loss bound.

The exact expectation formula for the least squares loss under volume sampling suggests a deep connection between linear regression and this distribution. We can use Theorem 3 to further strengthen that connection. Note, that the least squares estimator obtained through volume sampling can be written as 𝐰S∗=(𝐗𝐈S)+⁣⊤​𝐲\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*}=(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+\top}\mathbf{y}. Applying formula for the expectation of pseudo-inverse, we conclude that 𝐰S∗\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*} is an unbiased estimator of 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*}.

Proposition 7

Let 𝐗∈ℝd×n\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n} be a full-rank matrix and n≥s≥dn\geq s\geq d. Let S⊆1..nS\subseteq 1..n be a size ss volume sampled set over 𝐗\mathbf{X}. Then, for arbitrary label vector 𝐲∈ℝn\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, we have

𝔼⁡[𝐰S∗]=𝔼⁡[(𝐗𝐈S)+⁣⊤​𝐲]=𝐗+⁣⊤​𝐲=𝐰∗.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*}]=\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+\top}\mathbf{y}]=\mathbf{X}^{+\top}\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{w}^{*}.

Note, that the unbiasedness holds for volume sampling of any size, however the loss expectation formula is limited to size s=ds=d. Bounding the loss expectation for s>ds>d remains an open problem. However, we consider a different strategy for extending volume sampling in linear regression. Combining Proposition 7 with Theorem 5 we can compute the variance of predictions generated by volume sampling, and obtain tighter multiplicative loss bounds by sampling multiple dd-element subsets S1,…,StS_{1},...,S_{t} independently.

Theorem 8

Let (𝐗,𝐲)(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y}) be as in Theorem 5. For kk independent size dd volume samples S1,…,SkS_{1},\dots,S_{k}, we have

𝔼⁡[L⁡(1k​∑j=1k𝐰Sj∗)]=(1+dk)​L​(𝐰∗).\mathbb{E}\left[L\left(\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mathbf{w}_{S_{j}}^{*}\right)\right]=\left(1+\frac{d}{k}\right)\,L(\mathbf{w}^{*}).

Proof Denote 𝐲^=def𝐗⊤​𝐰∗\widehat{\mathbf{y}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{{def}}}}{{=}}\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{w}^{*} and 𝐲^S=def𝐗⊤​𝐰S∗\widehat{\mathbf{y}}_{S}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{{def}}}}{{=}}\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*} as the prediction vectors generated by 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*} and 𝐰S∗\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*} respectively. First, we perform bias-variance decomposition of the loss of 𝐰S∗\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*} (set SS is size dd volume sampled):

=𝔼⁡[‖𝐲^S−𝐲^‖2]+𝔼⁡[2​(𝐲^S−𝐲^)⊤​(𝐲^−𝐲)]+‖𝐲^−𝐲‖2\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\|\widehat{\mathbf{y}}_{S}-\widehat{\mathbf{y}}\|^{2}]+\mathbb{E}[2(\widehat{\mathbf{y}}_{S}-\widehat{\mathbf{y}})^{\top}(\widehat{\mathbf{y}}-\mathbf{y})]+\|\widehat{\mathbf{y}}-\mathbf{y}\|^{2}
=(∗)​∑i=1n𝔼⁡[(y^S,i−𝔼⁡[y^S,i])2]+L⁡(𝐰∗)=∑i=1nVar⁡[y^S,i]+L⁡(𝐰∗),\displaystyle\overset{(*)}{=}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}[(\widehat{y}_{S,i}-\mathbb{E}[\widehat{y}_{S,i}])^{2}]+L(\mathbf{w}^{*})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{y}_{S,i}]+L(\mathbf{w}^{*}),

where (∗)(*) follows from Theorem 3. Now, we use Theorem 5 to obtain the total variance of predictions:

∑i=1nVar⁡[y^S,i]=𝔼⁡[L⁡(𝐰S∗)]−L⁡(𝐰∗)=d​L​(𝐰∗).\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{y}_{S,i}]=\mathbb{E}[L(\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*})]-L(\mathbf{w}^{*})=d\;L(\mathbf{w}^{*}).

𝔼⁡[L⁡(1k​∑j=1k𝐰Sj∗)]\displaystyle\hskip 14.22636pt\mathbb{E}\left[L\left(\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mathbf{w}_{S_{j}}^{*}\right)\right] =∑i=1nVar⁡[1k​∑j=1ky^Sj,i]+L⁡(𝐰∗)\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{Var}\left[\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\widehat{y}_{S_{j},i}\right]+L(\mathbf{w}^{*})
=1k2​(∑j=1kd​L​(𝐰∗))+L⁡(𝐰∗)=(1+dk)​L​(𝐰∗). \displaystyle=\frac{1}{k^{2}}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{k}d\,L(\mathbf{w}^{*})\right)+L(\mathbf{w}^{*})=\left(1+\frac{d}{k}\right)L(\mathbf{w}^{*}).\hskip 56.9055pt\rule{6.45831pt}{6.45831pt}

It is worth noting that the average weight vector used in Theorem 8 is not expected to perform better than taking the solution to the joint subproblem, 𝐰S1:k∗\mathbf{w}_{S_{1:k}}^{*}, where S1:k=S1∪…∪SkS_{1:k}=S_{1}\cup...\cup S_{k}. However, theoretical guarantees for that case are not yet available.

4.1 Proof of Theorem 5

We use the following lemma regarding the leave-one-out loss for linear regression [3]:

Lemma 9

Let 𝐰−i∗\mathbf{w}_{-i}^{*} denote the least squares solution for problem (𝐗−i,𝐲−i)(\mathbf{X}_{-i},\mathbf{y}_{-i}). Then, we have

det(𝐗~​𝐗~⊤)\displaystyle\det(\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}^{\top}) =(1)​det(𝐗𝐗⊤)​‖𝐲^−𝐲‖2⏞L⁡(𝐰∗) where ​𝐗~=(𝐗𝐲⊤)\displaystyle\overset{(1)}{=}\det(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^{\top})\overbrace{\|\widehat{\mathbf{y}}-\mathbf{y}\|^{2}}^{L(\mathbf{w}^{*})}\qquad\text{ where }\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\mathbf{X}\\ \mathbf{y}^{\top}\end{array}\right)
=(2)​det(𝐗𝐗⊤)​(1−𝐱i⊤​(𝐗𝐗⊤)−1​𝐱i)​ℓi​(𝐰−i∗)\displaystyle\overset{(2)}{=}\det(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^{\top})(1-\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\top}(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{x}_{i})\ell_{i}(\mathbf{w}_{-i}^{*})
=(3)​det(𝐗−i​𝐗−i⊤)​ℓi​(𝐰−i∗),\displaystyle\overset{(3)}{=}\det(\mathbf{X}_{-i}\mathbf{X}_{-i}^{\top})\ell_{i}(\mathbf{w}_{-i}^{*}), (5)

where (1) is the “base ×\times height” formula for volume, (2) follows from Lemma 9 and (3) follows from a standard determinant formula. Returning to the proof, our goal is to find the expected loss 𝔼⁡[L⁡(𝐰S∗)]\mathbb{E}[L(\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*})], where SS is a size dd volume sampled set. First, we rewrite the expectation as follows:

=∑S,|S|=d∑j∉SProb⁡(S)​ℓj​(𝐰S∗)=∑T,|T|=d+1∑j∈TProb⁡(T−j)​ℓj​(𝐰T−j∗).\displaystyle=\sum_{S,|S|=d}\sum_{j\notin S}\mathrm{Prob}(S)\;\ell_{j}(\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*})=\sum_{T,|T|=d+1}\sum_{j\in T}\mathrm{Prob}(T_{-j})\;\ell_{j}(\mathbf{w}_{T_{-j}}^{*}). (6)

We now use (5) on the matrix 𝐗T\mathbf{X}_{T} and test instance 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j} (assuming rank⁡(𝐗T−j)=d\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X}_{T_{-j}})=d):

Prob⁡(T−j)​ℓj​(𝐰T−j∗)=det(𝐗T−j​𝐗T−j⊤)det(𝐗𝐗⊤)​ℓj​(𝐰T−j∗)=det(𝐗~T​𝐗~T⊤)det(𝐗𝐗⊤).\displaystyle\mathrm{Prob}(T_{-j})\;\ell_{j}(\mathbf{w}_{T_{-j}}^{*})=\frac{\det(\mathbf{X}_{T_{-j}}\mathbf{X}_{T_{-j}}^{\top})}{\det(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^{\top})}\;\ell_{j}(\mathbf{w}_{T_{-j}}^{*})=\frac{\det(\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_{T}\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_{T}^{\top})}{\det(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^{\top})}. (7)

Since the summand does not depend on the index j∈Tj\in T, the inner summation in (6) becomes a multiplication by d+1d+1. This lets us write the expected loss as:

𝔼⁡[L⁡(𝐰S∗)]=d+1det(𝐗𝐗⊤)​∑T,|T|=d+1det(𝐗~T​𝐗~T⊤)​=(1)​(d+1)​det(𝐗~​𝐗~⊤)det(𝐗𝐗⊤)​=(2)​(d+1)​L​(𝐰∗),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[L(\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*})]=\frac{d+1}{\det(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^{\top})}\sum_{T,|T|=d+1}\!\!\det(\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_{T}\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_{T}^{\top})\overset{(1)}{=}(d+1)\frac{\det(\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}^{\top})}{\det(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^{\top})}\overset{(2)}{=}(d+1)\,L(\mathbf{w}^{*}), (8)

where (1) follows from the Cauchy-Binet formula and (2) is an application of the “base ×\times height” formula. Thus the left-hand side of (7) is 00, while the right-hand side is non-negative, so (8) becomes an inequality, completing the proof of Theorem 5.

5 Efficient algorithm for volume sampling

In this section we propose an algorithm for efficiently performing exact volume sampling for any s≥ds\geq d. This addresses the question posed by [1], asking for a polynomial-time algorithm for the case when s>ds>d. [5, 10] gave an algorithm for the case when s=ds=d, which runs in time O⁡(n​d3)O(nd^{3}). Recently, [14] offered an algorithm for arbitrary ss, which has complexity O⁡(n4​s)O(n^{4}s). We propose a new method, which uses our techniques to achieve the time complexity O⁡((n−s+d)​n​d)O((n-s+d)nd), a direct improvement over [14] by a factor of at least n2n^{2}. Our algorithm also offers an improvement for s=ds=d in certain regimes. Namely, when n=o⁡(d2)n=o(d^{2}), then our algorithm runs in time O⁡(n2​d)=o⁡(n​d3)O(n^{2}d)=o(nd^{3}), faster than the method proposed by [5].

Our algorithm implements reverse iterative sampling from Corollary 2. After removing qq columns, we are left with an index set of size n−qn-q that is distributed according to volume sampling for column set size n−qn-q.

Theorem 10

Algorithm 1 runs in time O⁡((n−s+d)​n​d)O((n-s+d)nd), while using O⁡(d2+n)O(d^{2}+n) additional memory, and returns set SS which is distributed according to size ss volume sampling over 𝐗\mathbf{X}.

Proof For correctness we show the following invariants that hold at the beginning of the while loop:

pi=1−𝐱i⊤​(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)−1​𝐱i=(|S|−d)​P​(i|S)and𝐙=(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)−1.\displaystyle p_{i}=1-\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\top}(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{x}_{i}=(|S|-d)\,P(i|S)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbf{Z}=(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})^{-1}.

At the first iteration the invariants trivially hold. When updating the pjp_{j} we use 𝐙\mathbf{Z} and the pip_{i} from the previous iteration, so we can rewrite the update as

pj←pj−(𝐱j⊤​𝐯)2\displaystyle p_{j}\leftarrow p_{j}-(\mathbf{x}_{j}^{\top}\mathbf{v})^{2}
=1−𝐱j⊤​(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)−1​𝐱j−(𝐱j⊤​𝐙𝐱i)21−𝐱i⊤​(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)−1​𝐱i\displaystyle=1-\mathbf{x}_{j}^{\top}(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{x}_{j}-\frac{(\mathbf{x}_{j}^{\top}\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{x}_{i})^{2}}{1-\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\top}(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{x}_{i}}
=1−𝐱j⊤​(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)−1​𝐱j−𝐱j⊤​(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)−1​𝐱i​𝐱i⊤​(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)−1​𝐱j1−𝐱i⊤​(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)−1​𝐱i\displaystyle=1-\mathbf{x}_{j}^{\top}(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{x}_{j}-\frac{\mathbf{x}_{j}^{\top}(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{x}_{i}\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\top}(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{x}_{j}}{1-\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\top}(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{x}_{i}}
=1−𝐱j⊤​((𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)−1+(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)−1​𝐱i​𝐱i⊤​(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)−11−𝐱i⊤​(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)−1​𝐱i)​𝐱j\displaystyle=1-\mathbf{x}_{j}^{\top}\left((\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})^{-1}+\frac{(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{x}_{i}\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\top}(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})^{-1}}{1-\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\top}(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{x}_{i}}\right)\mathbf{x}_{j}
=(∗)​1−𝐱j⊤​(𝐗S−i​𝐗S−i)−1​𝐱j=(|S|−1−d)​P​(j|S−i),\displaystyle\overset{(*)}{=}1-\mathbf{x}_{j}^{\top}(\mathbf{X}_{S_{-i}}\mathbf{X}_{S_{-i}})^{-1}\mathbf{x}_{j}=(|S|-1-d)\,P(j|{S_{-i}}),

where (∗)(*) follows from the Sherman-Morrison formula. The update of 𝐙\mathbf{Z} is also an application of Sherman-Morrison and this concludes the proof of correctness.

Runtime: Computing the initial 𝐙=(𝐗𝐗⊤)−1\mathbf{Z}=(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^{\top})^{-1} takes O⁡(n​d2)O(nd^{2}), as does computing the initial values of pjp_{j}’s. Inside the while loop, updating pjp_{j}’s takes O⁡(|S|​d)=O⁡(n​d)O(|S|d)=O(nd) and updating 𝐙\mathbf{Z} takes O⁡(d2)O(d^{2}). The overall runtime becomes O⁡(n​d2+(n−s)​n​d)=O⁡((n−s+d)​n​d)O(nd^{2}+(n-s)nd)=O((n-s+d)nd). The space usage (in addition to the input data) is dominated by the pip_{i} values and matrix 𝐙\mathbf{Z}.  

6 Conclusions

We developed exact formulas for 𝔼[(𝐗𝐈S)+)]\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+})] and 𝔼[(𝐗𝐈S)+)2]\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{I}_{S})^{+})^{2}] when the subset SS of ss column indices is sampled proportionally to the volume det(𝐗S​𝐗S⊤)\det(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top}). The formulas hold for any fixed size s∈{d..n}s\in\{d..n\}. These new expectation formulas imply that the solution 𝐰S∗\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*} for a volume sampled subproblem of a linear regression problem is unbiased. We also gave a formula relating the loss of the subproblem to the optimal loss (ie 𝔼⁡(L⁡(𝐰S∗))=(d+1)​L​(𝐰∗)\mathbb{E}(L(\mathbf{w}_{S}^{*}))=(d+1)L(\mathbf{w}^{*})). However, this result only holds for sample size s=ds=d. It is an open problem to obtain such an exact expectation formula for s>ds>d.

A natural algorithm is to draw kk samples SiS_{i} of size dd and return 𝐰S1:k∗\mathbf{w}_{S_{1:k}}^{*}, where S1:k=⋃iSiS_{1:k}=\bigcup_{i}S_{i}. We were able to get exact expressions for the loss L⁡(1k​∑i𝐰Si)L(\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i}\mathbf{w}_{S_{i}}) of the average predictor but it is an open problem to get nontrivial bounds for the loss of the best predictor 𝐰S1:k∗\mathbf{w}_{S_{1:k}}^{*}.

We believe that our results demonstrate a fundamental connection between volume sampling and linear regression, which demands further exploration. Our loss expectation formula has already been applied by [17] to the task of linear regression without correspondence.
